# The Velocity Project

> A suite of TypeScript libraries for building software platforms end to end: a browser UI framework that creates real DOM elements (no virtual DOM), a themed component library, server-side TSX rendering, a web server, and a compact binary JSON wire format. They are written for Deno, published to JSR under @velotype, and developed in the Velotype GitHub organization (https://github.com/Velotype).

Each project stands on its own and they are designed to fit together: veloserver serves pages and APIs, velossr or Velotype renders them, velodesign supplies UI components for Velotype, and velojson (VSON) carries data between server and browser. The projects are pre-1.0, so APIs can change between versions: pin versions, and read each repository's release-notes.md.

## Read this before writing code with these libraries

- **Velotype is not React.** It has no virtual DOM, no reconciler, and no hooks (there is no useState or useEffect). A TSX tag evaluates to a real DOM element: `<div/>` is an HTMLDivElement. Components are classes that extend `Component`, state lives in class fields, and a value that changes is rendered in place by a `RenderObject`, `RenderBasic`, `RenderObjectArray`, or `RenderTemplateArray`. Do not call `refresh()` for routine updates: it throws away and rebuilds the component's children.
- **Attributes are HTML attributes.** Write `class`, not `className`. The `style` attribute takes an object only (a string has not type-checked since Velotype 0.0.25). Event attributes start with `on`: `onClick`.
- **Mount with `replaceElementWithRoot(<App/>, document.getElementById("app"))`.** Components are mounted by Velotype only when inserted through Velotype, not with `appendChild()`.
- **Server and browser TSX are different packages.** Browser code uses `"jsxImportSource": "@velotype/velotype"` and server code uses `"@velotype/velossr"`, so keep them in separate directories with their own deno.json.
- **Do not mix Velotype versions in one app.** A velodesign release is built on one Velotype version, and the Versions section below says which.
- **Conditionals:** `{condition && <li/>}` works in Velotype and in velossr 0.0.10 or later. In velomicro and velomini (and velossr before 0.0.10) a `false` child is written as the text "false", so use `{condition ? <li/> : null}`.
- **velodesign:** call `Theme.injectStyles()` once before any component renders. The library has no built-in text, so ARIA labels and placeholders have no defaults: pass them in.
- **veloserver:** `new Router<Metadata>({})`, add routes with `get`, `head`, and `post`, then `new Server(router).serve("127.0.0.1", 3000)`. Serving needs `--allow-net` and nothing else.
- **velojson:** `VSON.encode(value)` and `VSON.decode(bytes)`. The Key Table format is the default for objects and arrays. All three formats are smaller than JSON text (VBIN, which needs agreed key IDs, is the smallest), but on current engines they run slower than native JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse(), so choose them for payload size. The `/browser` module supports Key Table only.
- **velomicro and velomini** are small teaching frameworks (about 1kb and 2.5kb), not for applications. Use Velotype for an app.
- **Velotype DevTools** is a Chrome extension that is built from source and loaded unpacked. It is not a library.

## How to use these docs

Every docs page is available as Markdown at the links below. Every code example in the docs is a real file that is type-checked against the published package and then run, so prefer the docs' examples to code written from memory. If something is not in the docs, say so rather than guessing at an API.

## Versions

The docs and their examples were type-checked, and run, against these published versions:

- @velotype/velodesign 0.1.3: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velodesign
- @velotype/velojson 0.1.0: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velojson
- @velotype/velomicro 0.0.4: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velomicro
- @velotype/velomini 0.0.3: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velomini
- @velotype/veloserver 0.3.1: https://jsr.io/@velotype/veloserver
- @velotype/velossr 0.0.10: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velossr
- @velotype/velotype 0.3.1: https://jsr.io/@velotype/velotype

velodesign 0.1.3 is built on Velotype 0.3.1, so use that Velotype version with it.

# Getting started

velodesign is a themed component library for [Velotype](/docs/velotype/). Where HTML has an element for the job (`input`, `button`, `details`, `dialog`), the component is that element, so keyboard support, form participation, and browser autofill come from the platform. Colors come from a small set of CSS custom properties, so you can re-theme the whole library without touching a component.

This guide covers what the components have in common, and the parts of the library that are not components. For each component's props and a live preview, see the [showcase](https://velotype.github.io/velodesign/). The [components](/docs/velodesign/components/) page lists all of them, grouped by category, with a link to each.

Every example in these docs is a file that is type-checked against the published package, and run in a browser. This site is built with velodesign.

## Install

velodesign is a [JSR package](https://jsr.io/@velotype/velodesign) for Deno. It is built on Velotype, and velodesign 0.1.3 uses Velotype 0.3.1, so add both and use that Velotype version. Mixing Velotype versions in one app is not supported.

```sh
deno add jsr:@velotype/velotype@0.3.1 jsr:@velotype/velodesign@0.1.3
```

```json
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "jsx": "react-jsx",
        "jsxImportSource": "@velotype/velotype",
        "lib": ["dom", "deno.ns", "esnext"]
    }
}
```

## Use it

`Theme.injectStyles()` runs once, before any component renders. It sets up the CSS custom properties every component reads, and a small CSS reset. Then use components as tags in a Velotype app:

```tsx
import { Button, Checkbox, Stack, Theme } from "@velotype/velodesign"
import { replaceElementWithRoot } from "@velotype/velotype"

// Theme.injectStyles() runs once, before any component renders. It sets up the CSS custom
// properties every component reads, and a small CSS reset.
Theme.injectStyles()

replaceElementWithRoot(
    <Stack direction="column">
        <Checkbox>Enable notifications</Checkbox>
        <Button type="primary" onClick={() => console.log("clicked")}>Save</Button>
    </Stack>,
    document.getElementById("app")!,
)
```
## A tour

A few components from different categories, to show how they fit together. Form components are native elements with the usual attributes, feedback and overlay components show what happened, and `showToast()` is a function you call from a handler.

```tsx
import { Alert, Badge, Button, Card, Checkbox, Select, showToast, Stack, Tabs, Tag, TextBox, Tooltip } from "@velotype/velodesign"
import { replaceElementWithRoot } from "@velotype/velotype"

replaceElementWithRoot(
    <Stack direction="column">
        {/* Form: native inputs, buttons, and selects */}
        <Stack>
            <TextBox type="text" name="name" placeholder="Your name" required/>
            <Select name="role" placeholder="Choose a role" options={[
                {value: "admin", label: "Administrator"},
                {value: "user", label: "User"},
            ]}/>
            <Checkbox name="terms" checked>I agree</Checkbox>
        </Stack>
        <Stack>
            <Button type="primary" onClick={() => showToast("Saved", {type: "success", duration: 3000})}>Save</Button>
            <Button type="secondary">Cancel</Button>
            <Button type="danger" disabled>Delete</Button>
        </Stack>

        {/* Feedback */}
        <Alert type="warning" title="Heads up">This action cannot be undone.</Alert>

        {/* Data display */}
        <Card header="A card" footer={<Button type="text">Details</Button>}>
            <Badge type="primary">new</Badge> <Tag type="secondary">tagged</Tag>
        </Card>
        <Tabs tabs={[
            {key: "one", label: "One", content: <p>The first tab</p>},
            {key: "two", label: "Two", content: <p>The second tab</p>},
        ]}/>

        {/* Overlays */}
        <Tooltip content="More about this" placement="top"><Button type="text">Hover me</Button></Tooltip>
    </Stack>,
    document.getElementById("app")!,
)
```
## What is in the library

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| Typography | `Heading`, `Text`, `Paragraph`, `Icon` |
| Layout | `Stack`, `Grid` |
| Form | `Button`, `Checkbox`, `Select`, `TextBox`, `Textarea`, `Toggle`, `RadioButton` |
| Navigation | `Link`, `NavLink`, `Navbar`, `Sidebar`, `Breadcrumbs`, `Pagination`, `Menu`, `Steps` |
| Feedback | `Alert`, `Toast`, `Tooltip`, `Spinner`, `Progress`, `Skeleton`, `Empty` |
| Overlays | `Modal`, `Drawer`, `Popover`, `Popconfirm`, `ContextMenu`, `Command` |
| Data display | `Card`, `Table`, `DataTable`, `Tabs`, `Tree`, `Calendar`, `CodeBlock`, `Badge`, `Tag` |
| Data entry | `DatePicker`, `Slider`, `Combobox`, `Upload`, `Rate`, `Form` |
| Charts | `LineChart`, `AreaChart`, `BarChart`, `PieChart`, `Gauge`, `Sparkline` |

# Theming

Components get their colors from CSS custom properties, set on `<html>` by `Theme.injectStyles()`. Change the palette by passing colors, and every component follows. The theme also switches between light and dark.

## Colors

`Theme.injectStyles(options?, includeCSSReset = true)` takes a `ThemeColorOptions`. Every field is optional, and each color has a light value and a dark value:

| Color | Light option | Dark option | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| text | `textLightColor` | `textDarkColor` | Text |
| background | `backgroundLightColor`, `backgroundLightAltColor` | `backgroundDarkColor`, `backgroundDarkAltColor` | The page, and the surfaces on it |
| primary | `primaryLightColor` | `primaryDarkColor` | The main action and the current item |
| secondary | `secondaryLightColor` | `secondaryDarkColor` | A second accent |
| warning | `warningLightColor` | `warningDarkColor` | Cautions |
| accent | `accentLightColor` | `accentDarkColor` | Danger and errors |

The custom properties are:

* `--text` is the text color, and `--text-alt` is the opposite one
* `--background` is the page's color, `--background-1` to `--background-9` mix it toward `--background-alt` in steps, and `--background-alt` is the alternate. Components use the steps for borders, hovers, and the chrome around content
* `--primary`, `--secondary`, `--warning`, and `--accent` are the colors you set. `--primary-1` to `--primary-9` mix each toward white and black in steps, with `--primary-5` equal to `--primary`. Components use them for fills, borders, and hovers

You can use them in your own CSS, so your styles follow the theme too: `color: var(--primary-7)`.

`includeCSSReset` adds a small CSS reset. Pass `false` to leave your own in place.

## Light and dark

The theme is `light` or `dark`, set as `data-theme` on the `<html>` element. `ColorScheme` manages it:

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `getColorScheme()` | The scheme in effect: `"light"` or `"dark"`. A choice of `"default"` has already become one of these |
| `getColorSchemePreference()` | What the reader chose: `"light"`, `"dark"`, or `"default"`. A theme picker shows this one as selected, because `getColorScheme()` cannot tell a reader who chose light from one whose browser prefers it |
| `setColorScheme(scheme)` | Takes `"light"`, `"dark"`, or `"default"` to follow the browser's preference, and remembers it in `localStorage` |
| `resetColorScheme()` | Applies the stored choice, or the browser's preference when there is none |

`Theme.injectStyles()` applies the stored choice, or the browser's preference, to start.

## Theming part of a page

`setThemeOnSelector(selector, options?, resetSheet = false)` sets the same properties on any selector, not only `<html>`. The selected elements need `data-theme="light"` or `data-theme="dark"`.

It adds its stylesheet once per selector. Calling it again for the same selector with different options does nothing, unless `resetSheet` is `true`, which replaces the stylesheet. A live theme editor does this to preview changes.

```tsx
import { ColorScheme, setThemeOnSelector, Theme } from "@velotype/velodesign"

// Pass colors to change the palette. Every field is optional, and each has a light and a dark value.
// Each of primary, secondary, warning, and accent becomes a ramp of CSS variables: --primary is the
// color you gave, and --primary-1 to --primary-9 mix it toward white and black in steps, which
// components use for fills, borders, and hovers.
Theme.injectStyles({
    primaryLightColor: "#0b6bcb",
    primaryDarkColor: "#5aa9ff",
    accentLightColor: "#c4314b",
    accentDarkColor: "#ff6b81",
})

// The color scheme in effect is "light" or "dark", written to data-theme on <html>
console.log(ColorScheme.getColorScheme())

// setColorScheme() takes "light", "dark", or "default" (follow the browser's preference), and
// remembers the choice in localStorage
ColorScheme.setColorScheme("default")

// getColorScheme() is what is in effect, so "default" has already become "light" or "dark".
// getColorSchemePreference() is what the reader chose, "default" included, which is what a theme
// picker needs to show as selected.
console.log(ColorScheme.getColorScheme(), ColorScheme.getColorSchemePreference())

ColorScheme.setColorScheme("dark")
console.log(ColorScheme.getColorScheme(), ColorScheme.getColorSchemePreference())

// Go back to the stored choice, or the browser's preference when there is none
ColorScheme.resetColorScheme()

// Theme any part of the page, not only <html>. The selected elements need data-theme="light" or "dark".
const panel = document.createElement("section")
panel.className = "brand-panel"
panel.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark")
document.body.append(panel)
setThemeOnSelector(".brand-panel", {backgroundDarkColor: "#10202f"})

// Calling it again for the same selector does nothing unless resetSheet is true, which replaces the
// stylesheet. A live theme editor does this to preview changes.
setThemeOnSelector(".brand-panel", {backgroundDarkColor: "#201030"}, true)
```
## Symbols

A few small glyphs, such as a close control or a next arrow, are theme symbols. A symbol is a component with no attrs, so it can be an icon, an image, or text. The package's defaults are `✕` (close and cancel), `✓` (confirm), `∅` (empty), `…` (collapse), and `‹` and `›` (previous and next).

`CommonThemeOptions` holds the symbols that more than one component uses:

| Field | Used by |
|---|---|
| `closeSymbol` | `Alert`, `Toast`, `Tag`, `Modal`, `Drawer` |
| `cancelSymbol` | `Modal`'s footer, `Popconfirm`, an inline edit |
| `confirmSymbol` | `Popconfirm`, an inline edit, a completed `Steps` step |
| `emptySymbol` | `Empty`, the tables, every chart |
| `collapseSymbol` | `Breadcrumbs`, `Pagination` |
| `prevSymbol`, `nextSymbol` | `Pagination`, the calendars, `Carousel`, `AsyncDataTable` |

Each component also has its own options object, such as `AlertThemeOptions` and `ModalThemeOptions`. A field on it falls back to the common one until you assign it, so the common one sets all of them, and a component's own one overrides it for that component alone.

Assign symbols once at startup, before the first component that uses them is built. A symbol is a field on an object read when a component is built, not a CSS property, so changing one affects components built after it, and nothing re-renders. `resetThemeOptions(options, ...fields)` puts the package's defaults back, all of them or the named fields.

```tsx
import { Alert, AlertThemeOptions, CommonThemeOptions, Modal, ModalThemeOptions, resetThemeOptions } from "@velotype/velodesign"

// A theme symbol is a component with no attrs that the library draws for a small glyph, such as a
// close control. It is a field on an options object, not a CSS property, so assign it ONCE at
// startup, before the first component that uses it is built. There is no re-render when it changes.
CommonThemeOptions.closeSymbol = () => <b>x</b>   // Alert, Toast, Tag, Modal, Drawer
CommonThemeOptions.nextSymbol = () => <span>next</span>
CommonThemeOptions.prevSymbol = () => <span>back</span>

// A component's own options override the shared one for that component alone
ModalThemeOptions.closeSymbol = () => <b>close</b>
console.log(typeof AlertThemeOptions.closeSymbol)

// The package's defaults: ✕ ✓ ∅ … ‹ ›. resetThemeOptions() puts them back, all or by field.
resetThemeOptions(ModalThemeOptions)
resetThemeOptions(CommonThemeOptions, "nextSymbol", "prevSymbol")

document.body.append(<Alert type="info" onDismiss={() => {}} dismissLabel="Dismiss">An alert with a custom close</Alert>)
void Modal
```

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velodesign/layout-and-typography/

# Layout and typography

`Stack` and `Grid`, and `Heading`, `Text`, and `Paragraph`, are the primitives that everything else is composed from.

## Typography

* **`Heading`** renders `<h1>` to `<h6>`. `level` is required, because a default would quietly produce a second `<h1>` on a page that already has one. Size comes from the level, so the visual hierarchy and the document outline cannot disagree
* **`Text`** is inline text with modifiers: `strong`, `italic`, `underline`, `strike`, `numeric` (tabular figures, so digits line up and a changing value does not shift its neighbours), and `code` (a real `<code>` element)
* **`Paragraph`** is a block of prose with the package's line height and spacing
* **`type`** is a semantic color: `"muted"`, `"primary"`, `"secondary"`, `"warning"`, or `"danger"`. Leave it unset for the page's own text color. Use `type="muted"` for muted text: it is the right color in both themes

## Stack

`Stack` lays children out in a row or a column with a gap from one scale. It replaces `style={{display: "flex", gap: "0.5rem"}}`: every consumer spells it the same way, so two rows that look the same are the same.

| Attr | Values |
|---|---|
| `direction` | `"row"` (default) or `"column"` |
| `gap` | `"none"`, `"xs"` (0.25em), `"sm"` (0.5em), `"md"` (0.75em, default), `"lg"` (1.25em), `"xl"` (2em), or any CSS length |
| `align` | `"start"`, `"center"`, `"end"`, `"stretch"`, or `"baseline"`: how children line up across the stack |
| `justify` | `"start"`, `"center"`, `"end"`, `"between"`, or `"around"`: how children are spread along the stack |
| `wrap` | Let children wrap onto further lines (default: true for a row) |
| `inline` | Flow inline with surrounding text instead of taking a line of its own |

The gap scale is in `em`, not `px`, so spacing follows the type size.

A column `Stack` stretches its children, which is flexbox's own default. It is right for stacking cards or form fields, and surprising for badges. Use `align="start"` for those.

## Grid

`Grid` lays children out in columns.

| Attr | Description |
|---|---|
| `minColumnWidth` | Fit as many columns as will hold this width, then share the remainder (default: `"16em"`). It is `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(width, 1fr))`, so the grid reflows on its own, with no media query |
| `columns` | A fixed number of equal columns. Prefer `minColumnWidth` unless the count itself is meaningful, because a fixed count has to be chosen again at every breakpoint |
| `gap` | The same scale as `Stack` |
| `align` | How children line up within their cell |

```tsx
import { Grid, Heading, Paragraph, Stack, Text } from "@velotype/velodesign"
import { replaceElementWithRoot } from "@velotype/velotype"

replaceElementWithRoot(
    <Stack direction="column" gap="lg">
        {/* Typography. Heading requires a level, because a default would quietly produce a second <h1>. */}
        <Heading level={1}>A page</Heading>
        <Heading level={2} type="muted">A muted subheading</Heading>
        <Paragraph>Body text, with <Text strong>strong</Text>, <Text italic>italic</Text>, <Text underline>underline</Text>, <Text strike>strike</Text>, and <Text code>code</Text>.</Paragraph>
        <Paragraph>
            <Text type="muted">muted</Text> <Text type="primary">primary</Text> <Text type="secondary">secondary</Text> <Text type="warning">warning</Text> <Text type="danger">danger</Text>
        </Paragraph>
        <Text numeric>1,234.50</Text>

        {/* Stack: a row or a column, with a gap from a scale ("none" "xs" "sm" "md" "lg" "xl") or any CSS length */}
        <Stack>one<span>two</span><span>three</span></Stack>
        <Stack direction="column" gap="xs" align="start">
            <span>a column</span>
            <span>that does not stretch its children</span>
        </Stack>
        <Stack justify="between" align="center" gap="2rem" wrap={false}>
            <span>left</span><span>right</span>
        </Stack>
        <Stack inline gap="sm"><span>an inline</span><span>stack</span></Stack>

        {/* Grid: as many columns as fit minColumnWidth, with no media query. A fixed count is columns. */}
        <Grid minColumnWidth="10em" gap="md">
            <div>one</div><div>two</div><div>three</div><div>four</div>
        </Grid>
        <Grid columns={3} gap="sm" align="start">
            <div>one</div><div>two</div><div>three</div>
        </Grid>
    </Stack>,
    document.getElementById("app")!,
)
```

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velodesign/conventions/

# Conventions

What every component has in common, and the functions and objects around the components.

## Attrs

Every component's attrs type is named `<Name>AttrsType`, such as `ButtonAttrsType`, and exported. Each is built from shared pieces, which Velotype exports too:

* **`id`, `class`, and `style`** are accepted by components, and set on the element the component renders. `class` is added to the element's own classes rather than replacing them
* **`children`** are accepted by the components that take content, such as `Button`, `Card`, and `Alert`
* A component's own attrs are the rest

A component is a function component unless it needs state or a lifecycle, such as `Modal`, `Navbar`, and `TableOfContents`, which are classes. In TSX they are used the same way.

## Native elements

A component built on an element passes that element's attributes through, and uses the platform for the rest. A `Checkbox` is an `<input type="checkbox">` with a label, so it works with forms, keyboard, and autofill, and a `Modal` is a `<dialog>`.

## No language is assumed

The library has no built-in text. ARIA labels and placeholders have no default, because a default would be one language. Set the labels yourself, such as `dismissLabel` on an `Alert`, or `menuLabel` on a `Navbar`.

`S` is a store of strings by key, and `T` renders one, with an optional plural:

```tsx
import { LocalizedString, S, T } from "@velotype/velodesign"

// The library has no built-in text: it does not assume a language, so ARIA labels and
// placeholders have no default. S is a store of strings by key, and T renders one.
S.a("greeting", "Hello")

// A string with a plural form, chosen by a number
S.aS(new LocalizedString("items", "1 item", "many items"))

console.log(S.g("greeting"))     // Hello
console.log(S.g("items", 1))     // 1 item
console.log(S.g("items", 5))     // many items
console.log(S.g("missing"))      // -- missing --  (and an error is logged)

// <T k="..."/> renders a string in TSX, and n is the number for a plural
const message = <p><T k="greeting"/>, you have <T k="items" n={3}/></p>
document.body.append(message)
```
| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `S.a(key, value)` | Adds a string |
| `S.aS(localizedString)` | Adds a `LocalizedString`, which can have a plural form |
| `S.g(key, n?)` | Gets a string. With `n`, it chooses the plural form unless `n` is `1`. A missing key logs an error and returns `-- key --` |
| `<T k="key" n={n}/>` | Renders a string in TSX |

## Toasts and icons

`showToast(message, options?)` is a function, not a component, because a toast has no place in your tree. Call it from a handler. It keeps one container at the bottom right of the page. The options are `type`, `duration` (milliseconds before it is dismissed, default `4000`, and `0` keeps it), and `dismissLabel`.

An `Icon` is a width, a height, and an SVG path. `registerIcon(key, icon)` registers it, and `<I i={key}/>` renders it as an inline SVG, `1em` tall, in the current text color.

```tsx
import { Button, I, Icon, registerIcon, showToast } from "@velotype/velodesign"

// showToast() is a function, not a component: call it from a handler. It keeps one container at the
// bottom right of the page, and removes each toast after its duration (4000ms by default, 0 keeps it).
const toastButton = <Button type="primary" onClick={() => {
    showToast("Saved your changes", {type: "success"})
    showToast("Stays until dismissed", {type: "warning", duration: 0, dismissLabel: "Dismiss"})
}}>Show toasts</Button>

// An Icon is a width, a height, and an SVG path. Register it under a key, and render it with <I/>.
// It is drawn 1em tall in the current text color.
registerIcon("check", new Icon(24, 24, "M9 16.2 4.8 12l-1.4 1.4L9 19 21 7l-1.4-1.4z"))

document.body.append(toastButton, <p>Done <I i="check"/></p>, <I i="check" style={{height: "2em"}}/>)
```
## Routing

`Link` is a plain anchor, so open in a new tab, copy link address, and drag to a bookmark all work. Add `spa` and a click changes the location with `history.pushState()` instead of loading a page.

`NavLink` is a `Link` that knows whether it is the current page. It gets the class `vtd-nav-link-active`, or the `activeClass` you give it. `exact` is `true` by default, and matches the whole path. With `false` it matches any path that starts with `to`.

`History.changeLocation(path)` does a `pushState` and dispatches a `locationchange` event, which `NavLink` and `PageSelector` listen for. `History.loadNewPageLocation(path)` loads the page.

### Serving from a sub-path

An app that is not at the root of its domain, such as a GitHub Pages project site at `/my-repo/`, calls `History.configureBasePath("/my-repo")` once at startup. The app's own paths then leave the base path out: `Link` and `NavLink` add it to what they write, `NavLink` and `PageSelector` match against the path without it, and `changeLocation()` adds it. `History.getPathname()` is the location's path without the base path, and `History.resolveHref(path)` is a path with it.

```tsx
import { History, Link, NavLink, Navbar } from "@velotype/velodesign"

// An app served from a sub-path, such as a GitHub Pages project site at /my-repo/, sets its base path
// once at startup. Paths in the app then do not include it: Link and NavLink add it to hrefs, and
// getPathname() takes it off the location.
History.configureBasePath("/my-repo")
console.log(History.resolveHref("/docs/"))   // /my-repo/docs/
console.log(History.getPathname())           // the location's path, without /my-repo

// A Link is a plain anchor, so open-in-new-tab, copy-link, and drag-to-bookmark all work.
// spa makes a click change the location with history.pushState() instead of loading a page.
const links = <nav>
    <Link to="/docs/">A normal link</Link>
    <Link to="/docs/" spa>A client-side link</Link>
</nav>

// A NavLink is a Link that knows whether it is the current page: it gets the class
// "vtd-nav-link-active", or the one you give as activeClass. exact (default true) matches the whole
// path, and false matches any path that starts with it.
const nav = <Navbar brand={<NavLink to="/" spa>Home</NavLink>}>
    <NavLink to="/docs/" spa exact={false} activeClass="current">Docs</NavLink>
    <NavLink to="/about/" spa>About</NavLink>
</Navbar>

// Change the location from code. changeLocation() does a pushState and dispatches a "locationchange"
// event, which NavLink listens for. loadNewPageLocation() loads the page for real.
const button = <button type="button" onClick={() => History.changeLocation("/docs/")}>Go to docs</button>

document.body.append(nav, links, button)
```
## Updating only what changed

Components do the smallest DOM update that expresses a change, and none when nothing changed, so focus, caret position, text selection, scroll position, and running transitions survive. When you build on them, do the same: use [RenderObjects](/docs/velotype/render-objects/) rather than `refresh()` for state that changes.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velodesign/components/

# API reference

What `@velotype/velodesign` exports besides the [components](/docs/velodesign/components/). Each component exports its function or class and its `<Name>AttrsType`, and some export option types such as `ButtonType` and `TextType`.

## Theme

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `Theme.injectStyles(options?, includeCSSReset = true)` | Sets up the CSS custom properties and the reset |
| `setThemeOnSelector(selector, options?, resetSheet = false)` | Sets the properties on another selector |
| `ColorScheme.getColorScheme()` | The scheme in effect: `"light"` or `"dark"` |
| `ColorScheme.getColorSchemePreference()` | What the reader chose: `"light"`, `"dark"`, or `"default"` |
| `ColorScheme.setColorScheme(scheme)` | Sets and remembers `"light"`, `"dark"`, or `"default"` |
| `ColorScheme.resetColorScheme()` | Applies the stored choice or the browser's preference |
| `ThemeColorOptions` | The color options. See [Theming](/docs/velodesign/theming/#colors) |

## Symbols

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `CommonThemeOptions` | The symbols several components share: `closeSymbol`, `cancelSymbol`, `confirmSymbol`, `emptySymbol`, `collapseSymbol`, `prevSymbol`, `nextSymbol` |
| `AlertThemeOptions`, `BreadcrumbsThemeOptions`, `ButtonThemeOptions`, `ChartThemeOptions`, `DataTableThemeOptions`, `DrawerThemeOptions`, `EmptyThemeOptions`, `ModalThemeOptions`, `PaginationThemeOptions`, `PopconfirmThemeOptions`, `TagThemeOptions`, `TextFormFieldThemeOptions`, `ToastThemeOptions` | Each component's own options |
| `resetThemeOptions(options, ...fields)` | Puts the package's defaults back |
| `ThemeSymbol` | The type of a symbol: a component with no attrs |

See [Theming](/docs/velodesign/theming/#symbols).

## Strings

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `S.a`, `S.aS`, `S.g` | Add a string, add a `LocalizedString`, and get a string |
| `T` | `<T k="key" n={n}/>` renders a string |
| `LocalizedString` | `new LocalizedString(key, value, pluralValue?)` |

## Icons

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `Icon` | `new Icon(width, height, svgPath)` |
| `registerIcon(key, icon)` | Registers an icon |
| `I` | `<I i={key}/>` renders a registered icon |

## Routing and feedback

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `History.configureBasePath(path)` | Sets the path the app is served from, such as `"/my-repo"`. Call it once at startup |
| `History.getPathname()` | The location's path, without the base path |
| `History.resolveHref(path)` | A path with the base path added |
| `History.changeLocation(path)` | `pushState`, and dispatches `locationchange` |
| `History.loadNewPageLocation(path)` | Loads the page |
| `showToast(message, options?)` | Shows a toast. `ToastOptions`: `type`, `duration`, `dismissLabel` |

## Licenses

`addLicense(key, text)` adds the text of an open source license to `licenses`, a `Map` keyed by `key`. Each license is logged to the console once: those added in the first second after load are logged together, and later ones when they are added.

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/

# Getting started

velojson, or VSON (Velocity JSON), is a compact binary wire format for JavaScript JSON data. Any data representable with JSON in JavaScript is representable with VSON, and the other way around. No types or capabilities are added: it is a one-to-one mapping, so it can replace JSON between two programs without changing what they send.

To try it without installing anything, use the [playground](/projects/velojson/playground/), which encodes JSON to VSON and decodes bytes back to JSON in your browser.

Every example in these docs is a file that is type-checked against the published package and run, and the output shown is what the example printed.

## Install

velojson is a [JSR package](https://jsr.io/@velotype/velojson):

```sh
deno add jsr:@velotype/velojson
```

It has two modules:

| Import | For |
|---|---|
| `@velotype/velojson` | Servers. Optimized for speed, and supports every format: Base, Key Table, and VBIN |
| `@velotype/velojson/browser` | Browsers. Optimized for size (about 4.3kb minified), and supports the Key Table format only |

## Encode and decode

`VSON.encode(value)` returns a `Uint8Array`, and `VSON.decode(bytes)` returns the value. `decode()` reads the format from the data, so it takes no format argument.

```tsx
import { VSON } from "@velotype/velojson"

const startObj = { name: "Some name", age: 20, address: null }

// encode() returns a Uint8Array. Any JSON value can be encoded, and nothing else is added.
const objBinary: Uint8Array = VSON.encode(startObj)
console.log("VSON bytes:", objBinary.length)
console.log("JSON bytes:", JSON.stringify(startObj).length)

// decode() reads any VSON format, and returns the value
const endObj = VSON.decode(objBinary)
console.log(JSON.stringify(endObj))

// Every JSON value works, not only objects
for (const value of [null, true, 42, 3.14, "text", [1, 2, 3], {nested: {list: ["a", "b"]}}]) {
    const roundTripped = VSON.decode(VSON.encode(value))
    console.log(JSON.stringify(value), "->", JSON.stringify(roundTripped))
}

// undefined is handled as JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) handles it:
// an object key with the value undefined is left out, and undefined in an Array becomes null
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(VSON.encode({ a: 1, b: null, c: undefined }))))
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(VSON.encode([1, null, undefined]))))

// undefined itself encodes to zero bytes, and zero bytes decode to undefined
console.log(VSON.encode(undefined).length, VSON.decode(new Uint8Array()))
```
Output:

```text
VSON bytes: 34
JSON bytes: 44
{"name":"Some name","age":20,"address":null}
null -> null
true -> true
42 -> 42
3.14 -> 3.14
"text" -> "text"
[1,2,3] -> [1,2,3]
{"nested":{"list":["a","b"]}} -> {"nested":{"list":["a","b"]}}
{"a":1,"b":null}
[1,null,null]
0 undefined
```
### undefined

`undefined` is handled as `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))` handles it:

* An object key with the value `undefined` is left out
* `undefined` in an Array becomes `null`
* `undefined` passed directly to `encode()` is encoded in zero bytes, and zero bytes decode to `undefined`

## Which format?

`encode()` uses the Key Table format for an object or an Array, which is typically smaller than JSON. Choose another with the second argument. [Formats](/docs/velojson/formats/) compares them, and [VBIN](/docs/velojson/vbin/) covers the fast one.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/formats/

# Formats

VSON has three encoding formats. Each one solves a cost of the one before it. A message's format is written in its first byte, so `VSON.decode()` reads Base and Key Table messages without being told which.

| Format | `EncodingFormat` | Keys are | Needs agreement ahead of time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base | `EncodingFormat.Base` | written in full, each time | no |
| Key Table | `EncodingFormat.KeyTable` | written once, in a table at the end | no |
| VBIN | `EncodingFormat.KeyID` | not written, only numbered | yes: the KeyIDs |

## Base

A direct structural translation of JSON. Because it mirrors JSON's structure, it works for streaming and partial decoding. It is typically 20-25% smaller than the JSON text, and consistently smaller in nearly all cases.

## Key Table

All of an object's keys are collected into a table of strings appended to the root value, and each key in the data is a number that indexes the table. Every unique key is encoded once.

Compared with JSON text, it ranges from about 20% smaller, for a single object or many objects with mostly unique keys (where the table has little to deduplicate), up to about 65% smaller, for many records that share the same wide set of keys.

The root value must be an object or an Array. It is the default for those.

## VBIN

The Key Id format. It is like Key Table, but the table is not in the message. The encoder and decoder must already have agreed on a number for each key. VBIN is typically about 25% to 70% smaller than JSON text, following the same shape-dependent pattern, and it also skips the table's own overhead.

It also never encodes or decodes the key names as UTF-8 strings, or uses them as a string index on the constructed object. See [VBIN](/docs/velojson/vbin/).

## Comparing sizes

```tsx
import { EncodingFormat, VSON } from "@velotype/velojson"

// Many records that share the same keys: where the Key Table format helps most
const records = Array.from({length: 50}, (_, index) => ({
    id: index,
    firstName: "Ada",
    lastName: "Lovelace",
    emailAddress: `ada${index}@example.com`,
    isActive: index % 2 == 0,
}))
const json = JSON.stringify(records).length

// Base: a direct one-to-one translation of JSON. It can be streamed and partly decoded.
const base = VSON.encode(records, EncodingFormat.Base)

// KeyTable: every unique key is stored once, in a table at the end. It is the default for an
// object or an Array.
const keyTable = VSON.encode(records, EncodingFormat.KeyTable)
const byDefault = VSON.encode(records)

console.log("JSON text:", json, "bytes")
console.log("Base:     ", base.length, "bytes")
console.log("KeyTable: ", keyTable.length, "bytes")
console.log("The default is KeyTable:", byDefault.length == keyTable.length)

// decode() reads the format from the data, so it takes no format argument
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(base)) == JSON.stringify(records))
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(keyTable)) == JSON.stringify(records))

// KeyTable only supports an object or an Array at the root
try {
    VSON.encode("text", EncodingFormat.KeyTable)
} catch (error) {
    console.log((error as Error).message)
}
```
Output:

```text
JSON text: 5056 bytes
Base:      3893 bytes
KeyTable:  1988 bytes
The default is KeyTable: true
true
true
velojson: KeyTable encoding format only supported for root Object or Array types
```
## Speed

The formats are implemented in TypeScript, and typically run slower than the engine's native `JSON.stringify()` and `JSON.parse()`, which are heavily optimized. For the rare case of many complex numbers VSON outperforms them.

Choose them for the smaller payload: VSON when the encoder and decoder share nothing, and VBIN when they share a schema.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/vbin/

# VBIN

VBIN is the format for two programs that share a schema, such as a server and a client generated from the same definition. Instead of sending key names, or a table of them, it sends a number for each key, called a KeyID. It is the smallest of the three formats.

Because the KeyIDs are agreed ahead of time, using VBIN takes more code than `VSON.encode()`: you write the values with writers, and read them with a mapper.

## Writing

Create a `VBINRootWriter`, start the root object, write each value under its KeyID, and finalize the object. The root of a VBIN message must be an object.

| Writer | Writes |
|---|---|
| `VBINRootWriter` | The root: `startRootObject()`, `finalizeRootObject(object)`, and `toUint8ArrayAndRelease()` |
| `VBINObjectWriter` | An object's fields: `encodePosIntValue`, `encodeDoubleValue`, `encodeNumberValue`, `encodeStringValue`, `encodeBooleanValue`, and the `finalize...` methods for nested values |
| `VBINArrayWriter` | An Array of mixed values |
| `VBINNumberArrayWriter` | An Array of numbers, some integers and some doubles |
| `VBINHomogenousStringArrayWriter` | An Array of only strings |
| `VBINHomogenousPosIntArrayWriter` | An Array of only non-negative integers |
| `VBINHomogenousDoubleArrayWriter` | An Array of only doubles |
| `VBINHomogenousObjectArrayWriter` | An Array of only objects |

An array or a nested object is written with its own writer, and then finalized into its parent under a KeyID: `finalizeArray`, `finalizeNumberArray`, `finalizeHomogenousStringArray`, `finalizeHomogenousPosIntArray`, `finalizeHomogenousDoubleArray`, `finalizeHomogenousObjectArray`, and `finalizeObject`.

The `encode...Value` methods of an object accept `undefined`, which writes nothing, as an `undefined` key is left out in the other formats.

## Reading

`VBIN.decode(bytes, mapper)` reads a message with a `VBINObjectMapper`, which maps each KeyID back to a field:

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `assignValue(object, keyID, value)` | Sets the field for `keyID` on the object being built |
| `hasAllRequiredFields(object)` | Called at the end of an object. Return `false` to reject a message with a missing field. `decode()` then throws |
| `fieldMapper(keyID)` | For a field that is itself an object, returns the mapper for its fields |

```tsx
import {
    VBIN,
    type VBINObjectMapper,
    VBINObjectWriter,
    VBINHomogenousStringArrayWriter,
    VBINRootWriter,
    VSON,
} from "@velotype/velojson"

// VBIN does not send key names. The encoder and decoder agree on a number for each key (a KeyID)
// ahead of time, which is why it is smaller and faster than the other formats.
type Product = {
    id: number        // KeyID 1
    name: string      // KeyID 2
    inStock: boolean  // KeyID 3
    tags: string[]    // KeyID 4
}

const product: Product = {id: 7, name: "Widget", inStock: true, tags: ["tools", "metal"]}

// Encode with writers. Each value is written under its KeyID.
function encodeProduct(product: Product): Uint8Array {
    const root = new VBINRootWriter()
    const object: VBINObjectWriter = root.startRootObject()
    object.encodePosIntValue(1, product.id)
    object.encodeStringValue(2, product.name)
    object.encodeBooleanValue(3, product.inStock)

    // An array is written with its own writer, and then finalized into the object under a KeyID
    const tags = new VBINHomogenousStringArrayWriter()
    product.tags.forEach(tag => tags.encodeStringValueInHomogenousArray(tag))
    object.finalizeHomogenousStringArray(4, tags)

    root.finalizeRootObject(object)
    return root.toUint8ArrayAndRelease()
}

// Decode with a mapper that turns each KeyID back into a field
const productMapper: VBINObjectMapper = {
    assignValue: (object, keyID, value) => {
        switch (keyID) {
            case 1: object.id = value; break
            case 2: object.name = value; break
            case 3: object.inStock = value; break
            case 4: object.tags = value; break
        }
    },
    // Called at the end of an object: return false to reject it, such as when a field is missing
    hasAllRequiredFields: (object) => object.id !== undefined && object.name !== undefined,
    // For a field that is itself an object, return the mapper for its KeyID
    fieldMapper: () => undefined,
}

const bytes = encodeProduct(product)
console.log("VBIN bytes:", bytes.length)
console.log("VSON bytes:", VSON.encode(product).length)
console.log("JSON bytes:", JSON.stringify(product).length)

const decoded: Product = VBIN.decode(bytes, productMapper)
console.log(JSON.stringify(decoded))

// VSON.decode() reads VBIN too, in a debug format: a plain object keyed by KeyID
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(bytes)))

// A message that is missing a required field is rejected
const incomplete = new VBINRootWriter()
const empty = incomplete.startRootObject()
empty.encodePosIntValue(1, 1)
incomplete.finalizeRootObject(empty)
try {
    VBIN.decode(incomplete.toUint8ArrayAndRelease(), productMapper)
} catch (error) {
    console.log("rejected:", (error as Error).message)
}
```
Output:

```text
VBIN bytes: 28
VSON bytes: 51
JSON bytes: 64
{"id":7,"name":"Widget","inStock":true,"tags":["tools","metal"]}
{"1":7,"2":"Widget","3":true,"4":["tools","metal"]}
rejected: velojson: missing required field
```
## Debugging

`VSON.decode()` reads a VBIN message too, in a debug format: a plain object keyed by KeyID, such as `{"1": 7, "2": "Widget"}`. This is what the [VeloJSON panel](/docs/velotype/devtools/) of the DevTools extension shows for a VBIN payload.

## Generating the code

Writers and mappers are repetitive, and must agree with each other. Generate them from a schema rather than writing them by hand.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/browser/

# Browser module

`@velotype/velojson/browser` is the same format in a smaller module, about 4.3kb minified. It supports only the Key Table format, which `VSON.encode()` uses for an object or an Array, so it has no encoding format argument, and no VBIN writers or mapper.

Its `VSON.decode()` reads Key Table data. Its output is the same bytes as the server module's, so either side can decode what the other encodes.

```tsx
// The browser module is tuned for size (about 4.3kb minified) rather than speed. It supports the
// KeyTable format only, which is what VSON.encode() uses for an object or an Array.
import { VSON } from "@velotype/velojson/browser"
import { VSON as ServerVSON } from "@velotype/velojson"

const message = {user: "ada", items: [{id: 1, label: "one"}, {id: 2, label: "two"}]}

const bytes = VSON.encode(message)
console.log(bytes.length, "bytes")
console.log(JSON.stringify(VSON.decode(bytes)))

// It produces the same bytes as the server module, so either side can decode what the other encodes
const serverBytes = ServerVSON.encode(message)
console.log("same bytes as the server module:", bytes.length == serverBytes.length && bytes.every((byte, index) => byte == serverBytes[index]))
console.log(JSON.stringify(ServerVSON.decode(bytes)))
```
Output:

```text
48 bytes
{"user":"ada","items":[{"id":1,"label":"one"},{"id":2,"label":"two"}]}
same bytes as the server module: true
{"user":"ada","items":[{"id":1,"label":"one"},{"id":2,"label":"two"}]}
```
Use it for sending data to a server and reading a server's responses in a browser, with the [Velotype DevTools](/docs/velotype/devtools/) extension to inspect them.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/wire-format/

# Wire format

The format of each message, for implementing VSON in another language or reading bytes by hand.

## Values

Every value is a `VStruct` that starts with one varint, `A`, built from a key (or key length) and a 3 bit wire type:

| Wire type | Value | Encoded value that follows |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `null` | none |
| 1 | `false` | none |
| 2 | `true` | none |
| 3 | positive integer | a positive varint (1 to 7 bytes), for zero and up to `Number.isSafeInteger()` |
| 4 | double | 8 bytes, little endian, for any other number |
| 5 | string | a length varint, then UTF-8 bytes |
| 6 | object | a length varint, then a series of `VStruct`s, each with a key |
| 7 | array | a length varint with a homogenous bit, then `VStruct`s with no key |

The bytes of a few values, in the Base format:

```tsx
import { EncodingFormat, VSON } from "@velotype/velojson"

// The bytes of a few values in the Base format, to read alongside the format specification.
// Each value starts with a varint: the encoding format (0 for Base) shifted past 3 bits of wire type.
const show = (label: string, value: unknown) => {
    const bytes = VSON.encode(value, EncodingFormat.Base)
    console.log(label.padEnd(12), [...bytes].map(byte => byte.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join(" "))
}

show("null", null)           // wire type 0
show("false", false)         // wire type 1
show("true", true)           // wire type 2
show("42", 42)               // wire type 3: a positive integer, as a varint
show("1.5", 1.5)             // wire type 4: a double, 8 bytes little endian
show('"hi"', "hi")           // wire type 5: a length, then UTF-8
show("[]", [])               // wire type 7
show("{}", {})               // wire type 6
show('{"a":1}', {a: 1})      // a key length and wire type, the key, then the value
```
```text
null         00
false        01
true         02
42           03 2a
1.5          04 00 00 00 00 00 00 f8 3f
"hi"         05 02 68 69
[]           07 00
{}           06 00
{"a":1}      06 03 0b 61 01
```
Reading them: the root of `{"a":1}` is `06` (format 0, wire type 6: an object), `03` (the body is 3 bytes), `0b` (key length 1, wire type 3: a positive integer), `61` (the key `a`), and `01` (the value).

## Base

`VRoot` is `{A: encoding format (0) ++ wire type}{C?: encoded value}`.

`VStruct` is `{A: key length ++ wire type}{B?: key}{C?: encoded value}`, where `A` is a positive varint of the key's length in bytes followed by 3 bits for the wire type, `B` is the UTF-8 key (absent for the root and for array items), and `C` is the encoded value. In the Base format a key length of zero encodes the empty-string key `""`.

### Arrays

An array is `{A}{B?}{C}` with `C` as `{LENGTH ++ 0}{VALUE?}` for a heterogenous array, or `{LENGTH ++ 1}{WIRETYPE}{VALUE}` for a homogenous one. `LENGTH` is a positive varint. A homogenous array's values all have one wire type, which is written once, and skip their own wire type byte. The encoder may choose either encoding for a homogenous array.

## Key Table

`VRoot` is `{A: encoding format (1) ++ wire type}{C: encoded value}{D: encoded key table}`, and the root must be an object or an Array.

Keys are replaced by a 1-indexed key index into the table: `VStruct` is `{A: key index ++ wire type}{C?: encoded value}`, where an index of zero means no key. `D` is a homogenous string array of all the keys.

## VBIN

`VRoot` is `{A: encoding format (2) ++ wire type}{C: encoded value}`, and the root must be an object.

`VStruct` is `{A: key index ++ wire type}{C?: encoded value}`, where the key index is the KeyID, which the encoder and decoder agreed on ahead of time. There is no key table.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velojson/api-reference/

# API reference

## @velotype/velojson

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| [`VSON.encode(value, encodingFormat?)`](/docs/velojson/#encode-and-decode) | Encodes any JSON value to a `Uint8Array`. The format defaults to Key Table for an object or an Array, and Base otherwise. Throws on an error |
| `VSON.decode(data)` | Decodes Base and Key Table data (and VBIN, in the debug format). Returns `undefined` for zero bytes |
| [`VBIN.decode(data, mapper)`](/docs/velojson/vbin/#reading) | Decodes VBIN data with a `VBINObjectMapper` |
| `EncodingFormat` | An enum: `Base` (0), `KeyTable` (1), `KeyID` (2) |
| `WireType` | An enum: `Null`, `False`, `True`, `PosInt`, `Double`, `String`, `Object`, `Array` |
| `JSONValue` | `null \| boolean \| number \| string \| JSONValue[] \| {[key: string]: JSONValue}` |
| `VBINObjectMapper` | `{assignValue, hasAllRequiredFields, fieldMapper}` |
| [VBIN writers](/docs/velojson/vbin/#writing) | `VBINRootWriter`, `VBINObjectWriter`, `VBINArrayWriter`, `VBINNumberArrayWriter`, `VBINHomogenousStringArrayWriter`, `VBINHomogenousPosIntArrayWriter`, `VBINHomogenousDoubleArrayWriter`, `VBINHomogenousObjectArrayWriter` |

### VBINRootWriter

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `startRootObject(): VBINObjectWriter` | Starts the root object |
| `finalizeRootObject(childWriter)` | Ends the root object |
| `toUint8ArrayAndRelease(): Uint8Array` | The bytes. The writer is released |

### VBINObjectWriter

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `encodeBooleanValue(keyID, value)` | A boolean |
| `encodePosIntValue(keyID, value)` | A non-negative integer |
| `encodeDoubleValue(keyID, value)` | A double |
| `encodeNumberValue(keyID, value)` | A number, as an integer or a double |
| `encodeStringValue(keyID, value)` | A string |
| `finalizeObject(keyID, childWriter)` | A nested object |
| `finalizeArray(keyID, childWriter)` | A mixed Array |
| `finalizeNumberArray(keyID, childWriter)` | An Array of numbers |
| `finalizeHomogenousStringArray(keyID, childWriter)` | An Array of strings |
| `finalizeHomogenousPosIntArray(keyID, childWriter)` | An Array of non-negative integers |
| `finalizeHomogenousDoubleArray(keyID, childWriter)` | An Array of doubles |
| `finalizeHomogenousObjectArray(keyID, childWriter)` | An Array of objects |
| `toUint8Array()`, `release()` | The bytes so far, and releasing the writer |

The array writers have matching `encode...InArray` and `encode...InHomogenousArray` methods, such as `VBINArrayWriter.encodeStringValueInArray(value)` and `VBINHomogenousPosIntArrayWriter.encodePosIntValueInHomogenousArray(value)`, and `VBINHomogenousObjectArrayWriter.finalizeObjectInHomogenousArray(childWriter)`.

## @velotype/velojson/browser

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `VSON.encode(value)` | Encodes an object or an Array in the Key Table format |
| `VSON.decode(data)` | Decodes Key Table data |
| `WireType` | The wire types, as a plain object |
| `JSONValue` | The type of an encodable value |

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velomicro/

# Getting started

velomicro is a strictly minimal TSX framework, about 1kb, that shows how TSX rendering works. It is small enough to read in one sitting: a `createElement` that returns real DOM elements, and function components. The [Medium article](https://argoday.medium.com/a-1kb-tsx-framework-to-demonstrate-how-tsx-works-velotype-tsx-micro-337c32ff0648) walks through its source line by line.

It is a teaching tool and a starting point, not a framework for an app. It has no state management and no lifecycle. For an app, see [Velotype](/docs/velotype/), which keeps this model of TSX that returns real elements, and adds the rest. [velomini](/docs/velomini/) is the next step up.

Every example in these docs is a file that is type-checked against the published package, and run in a browser.

## Install

velomicro is a [JSR package](https://jsr.io/@velotype/velomicro) for Deno:

```sh
deno add jsr:@velotype/velomicro
```

```json
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "jsx": "react-jsx",
        "jsxImportSource": "@velotype/velomicro"
    }
}
```

## How it works

Each tag is a call to `createElement`, which creates a real `HTMLElement`, sets its attributes, and appends its children. So a tag's value is the element:

```tsx
// Every tag evaluates to a real HTMLElement
const divTag: HTMLDivElement = <div>this is a div</div>

// Attributes are set with setAttribute(), so you write TSX the way you write HTML
const withClass: HTMLDivElement = <div class="exampleClass" id="main">this has a class</div>

// style takes an object, with camelCase keys, or a string
const styleObject: HTMLDivElement = <div style={{display: "inline", marginTop: "4px"}}>an object of styles</div>
const styleString: HTMLDivElement = <div style="display:inline;margin-top:4px;">a string of styles</div>

// Attributes that start with "on" add event listeners
const clicked: HTMLButtonElement = <button type="button" onClick={() => console.log("clicked")}>Click me</button>

// A boolean attribute is set empty when true, and left out when false
const input: HTMLInputElement = <input type="checkbox" checked={true} disabled={false}/>

// Fragments group children without a wrapper element, and arrays of elements are children too
const items = <><li>one</li><li>two</li></>
const list: HTMLUListElement = <ul>{items}{["three", "four"].map(name => <li>{name}</li>)}</ul>

// null and undefined render nothing. A boolean child is written as text, so for a condition use a
// ternary that gives null rather than {condition && <div/>}, which writes "false".
const signedIn = false
const conditional: HTMLDivElement = <div>{signedIn ? <span>Account</span> : null}</div>

document.body.append(divTag, withClass, styleObject, styleString, clicked, input, list, conditional)
```
* **Attributes** are set with `setAttribute()`, so you write them as you would in HTML (`class`, not `className`)
* **Attributes that start with `on`** add event listeners
* **`style`** takes an object with camelCase keys, or a string
* **Boolean attributes** are set empty when `true` and left out when `false`
* **Children** can be elements, strings, numbers, and arrays of them. Fragments (`<>...</>`) return their children as an array
* **`null` and `undefined`** render nothing. A boolean child is written as text, so `{condition && <div/>}` writes `false` when the condition is false. Use `{condition ? <div/> : null}`

## Function components

A function component is a function from its attrs to an element, and it receives its children as a second argument.

```tsx
import type { ChildrenAttr, FunctionComponent, IdAttr, StylePassthroughAttrs } from "@velotype/velomicro/tsx-micro"

type GreetingAttrsType = {name: string}

// A function component receives its attrs, and its children as a second argument
const Greeting: FunctionComponent<GreetingAttrsType> = function(attrs: GreetingAttrsType) {
    return <div>Hello {attrs.name}!</div>
}

// ChildrenAttr, IdAttr, and StylePassthroughAttrs describe the children, id, class, and style that
// a component accepts and passes on to the element it renders
type PanelAttrsType = {title: string} & ChildrenAttr & IdAttr & StylePassthroughAttrs

const Panel: FunctionComponent<PanelAttrsType> = function(attrs: PanelAttrsType, children) {
    return <section id={attrs.id} class={attrs.class} style={attrs.style}>
        <h2>{attrs.title}</h2>
        {children}
    </section>
}

document.body.append(
    <Panel title="Greetings" id="greetings" class="panel" style={{marginTop: "8px"}}>
        <Greeting name="Ada"/>
        <Greeting name="Grace"/>
    </Panel>,
)
```
The attrs helper types are `EmptyAttrs` (no attrs), `ChildrenAttr`, `IdAttr`, and `StylePassthroughAttrs` (`class` and `style`). They describe what a component accepts and passes on, and a component passes them on itself.

## A counter

A function component runs once. Its state is a variable, and updating the page is up to you: here, by changing the label element.

```tsx
import type { EmptyAttrs, FunctionComponent } from "@velotype/velomicro/tsx-micro"

// A function component returns an element. State is a variable, and updating the page is up to you.
const Counter: FunctionComponent<EmptyAttrs> = function(_attrs: EmptyAttrs): HTMLDivElement {
    let count = 0
    const counterLabel = <span>{count}</span>
    return <div>
        <div>Counter value: {counterLabel}</div>
        <button type="button" onClick={() => {
            count += 1
            counterLabel.innerText = String(count)
        }}>Increment</button>
        <button type="button" onClick={() => {
            count -= 1
            counterLabel.innerText = String(count)
        }}>Decrement</button>
    </div>
}

// TSX returns real elements, so mounting is appending
document.body.append(<Counter/>)
```
This is the limit of velomicro. When you need a value that updates the page for you, a lifecycle, or classes, move up to [velomini](/docs/velomini/) or [Velotype](/docs/velotype/).

## The classic runtime

The automatic JSX runtime is `@velotype/velomicro`. With the classic transform, `h` and `f` from `@velotype/velomicro/tsx-micro` are what tags and fragments compile to:

```tsx
/** @jsxRuntime classic */
/** @jsx h */
/** @jsxFrag f */
// With the classic JSX transform, `h` and `f` are what tags and fragments compile to: createElement
// and createFragment, with short names. Set them per file with the pragmas above, or with
// "jsx": "react", "jsxFactory": "h", and "jsxFragmentFactory": "f" in deno.json.
import { f, h } from "@velotype/velomicro/tsx-micro"

const list = <ul><li>one</li><li>two</li></ul>
const fragment = <><span>a</span><span>b</span></>

document.body.append(list, ...fragment)
```
## API

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `h(tag, attrs, ...children)` | `createElement`: creates an element, sets its attributes, and appends its children |
| `f(attrs, ...children)` | `createFragment`: returns its children as an array |
| `jsx`, `jsxs`, `Fragment` | The automatic JSX runtime. `jsx` and `jsxs` are the same |
| `FunctionComponent<AttrsType>` | `(attrs, children) => RenderableElements` |
| `RenderableElements` | `BasicTypes \| HTMLElement \| RenderableElements[] \| null \| undefined` |
| `BasicTypes` | `string \| bigint \| number \| boolean` |
| `EmptyAttrs`, `ChildrenAttr`, `IdAttr`, `StylePassthroughAttrs` | Attrs helper types |

Imports: `@velotype/velomicro` is the runtime, and `@velotype/velomicro/tsx-micro` has `h`, `f`, and the types. In velomicro the JSX types accept any attribute on any element.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/velomini/

# Getting started

velomini is a mostly minimal TSX framework, about 2.5kb, that adds class components to [velomicro](/docs/velomicro/): a `Component` base class with `render()`, `mount()`, `unmount()`, and `refresh()`. Its way to update what is on screen is to tear down a component's subtree and render a new one, with no diffing and no patching. The [Medium article](https://argoday.medium.com/a-2-5kb-tsx-framework-that-adds-classes-velomini-6f65cd979d40) walks through its source.

It is a teaching tool. [Velotype](/docs/velotype/) is the full framework: it keeps classes and the real-element model, and replaces `refresh()` with values that update in place.

Every example in these docs is a file that is type-checked against the published package, and run in a browser.

## Install

velomini is a [JSR package](https://jsr.io/@velotype/velomini) for Deno:

```sh
deno add jsr:@velotype/velomini
```

```json
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "jsx": "react-jsx",
        "jsxImportSource": "@velotype/velomini"
    }
}
```

## Everything from velomicro

velomini's TSX works as [velomicro](/docs/velomicro/)'s does: tags create real elements, attributes are HTML attributes, `style` takes an object, `on` attributes add listeners, and function components are functions of their attrs and children. As in velomicro, a boolean child is written as text, so use `{condition ? <div/> : null}` rather than `{condition && <div/>}`.

## Class components

A class component extends `Component<AttrsType>` and implements `render(attrs, children)`. It is created as a tag, and its attrs are the tag's attributes.

`getComponent<T>(element)` converts an element that was created for a class back to the instance, so you can call its methods. The element is still usable in TSX.

```tsx
import { Component, type EmptyAttrs, getComponent, replaceElement } from "@velotype/velomini/tsx-mini"

// Define a class. Its attrs are the type parameter, and render() returns what it shows.
class ComplexComponent extends Component<{foo: string}> {
    override render(attrs: Readonly<{foo: string}>) {
        return <div>Hello {attrs.foo}</div>
    }
}

// Create it as a tag
const page = <div><ComplexComponent foo="Component!"></ComplexComponent></div>

// Class Components can have methods. getComponent() converts an element that was created for a
// class back to the instance, to call them.
class Advanced extends Component<EmptyAttrs> {
    override render() {
        return <div>This is an advanced Component</div>
    }
    someMethod() {
        console.log("Advanced someMethod() called")
    }
}
const advanced: Advanced = getComponent<Advanced>(<Advanced/>)
advanced.someMethod()

// Mount the page by replacing a placeholder element
const placeholder = document.createElement("div")
document.body.append(placeholder)
replaceElement(placeholder, <div>{page}{advanced}</div>)
```
## Mounting

`replaceElement(element, newElement)` replaces an element with a new one, and mounts what is inside the new one. Use it to put an app on the page: insert a placeholder element, then replace it. It returns the new element, and if the old element had focus the new one is focused.

## The lifecycle

| Method | Called |
|---|---|
| `render(attrs, children)` | When the component needs to be turned into elements |
| `mount()` | Just after the component is attached to the DOM, children before parents |
| `unmount()` | Just before the component is removed from the DOM |
| `refresh()` | By you: unmounts and deletes the component's children, renders it again, and mounts the new children |

`replaceElement()` mounts the components inside the new element and unmounts the components inside the element it replaces. A component that is itself the new element is not mounted, so wrap it in an element, as `<main>` is wrapped here:

```tsx
import { Component, type EmptyAttrs, replaceElement } from "@velotype/velomini/tsx-mini"

class Clock extends Component<EmptyAttrs> {
    time = new Date().toLocaleTimeString()
    timer?: number

    // Called just after the Component is attached to the DOM
    override mount() {
        console.log("mounted")
        this.timer = setInterval(() => {
            this.time = new Date().toLocaleTimeString()
            // Unmounts and deletes the Component's children, and renders it again from scratch
            this.refresh()
        }, 1000)
    }

    // Called just before the Component is removed from the DOM
    override unmount() {
        console.log("unmounted")
        clearInterval(this.timer)
    }

    override render() {
        return <div>The time is {this.time}</div>
    }
}

const placeholder = document.createElement("div")
document.body.append(placeholder)
// replaceElement() mounts the Components inside the new element, children before parents, and
// unmounts the Components inside the element it replaces. A Component that is itself the new
// element is not mounted, so wrap it in an element as <main> is wrapped here.
const root = replaceElement(placeholder, <main><Clock/></main>)
replaceElement(root, <main>Removed</main>)
```
Because `refresh()` rebuilds everything inside the component, anything those children held (text typed into an input, focus, a nested component's state) is lost. This is the cost that Velotype's [RenderObjects](/docs/velotype/render-objects/) remove.

## Other functions

`setAttrsOnElement(element, attrs)` sets attributes, a style object, event listeners, and boolean attributes on an existing element, the way TSX does.

```tsx
import { replaceElement, setAttrsOnElement } from "@velotype/velomini/tsx-mini"

// setAttrsOnElement() sets attributes, a style object, event listeners, and boolean attributes on
// an existing element, the way TSX does
const input = document.createElement("input")
setAttrsOnElement(input, {
    type: "text",
    class: "wide",
    style: {width: "100%"},
    onInput: () => console.log("typed"),
    required: true,
})
document.body.append(input)

// replaceElement() replaces an element with a new one. If the old element had focus, the new one
// is given it. It returns the new element.
input.focus()
const replacement = replaceElement(input, <input type="text" class="replacement"/>)
console.log(document.activeElement == replacement)
```
## API

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `Component<AttrsType>` | The abstract base class: `render()`, `mount()`, `unmount()`, `refresh()`, and `vtKey` and `element`, which the framework sets |
| `getComponent<T>(element)` | The class instance behind an element |
| `replaceElement(element, newElement)` | Replaces an element and mounts the new one's components |
| `setAttrsOnElement(element, attrs)` | Sets attributes on an existing element |
| `h`, `f`, `jsx`, `jsxs`, `Fragment` | The JSX runtimes |
| `FunctionComponent<AttrsType>` | `(attrs, children) => RenderableElements` |
| `RenderableElements`, `BasicTypes`, `EmptyAttrs`, `ChildrenAttr`, `IdAttr`, `StylePassthroughAttrs` | The types |
| `__vtAppMetadata` | Internal state for debugging. Do not use it |

Imports: `@velotype/velomini` is the runtime, and `@velotype/velomini/tsx-mini` has the classes, functions, and types.

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/veloserver/

# Getting started

veloserver is a web server framework for Deno. It has a typed router, per-request metadata, inspectors that run before and after handlers, static file serving, and a development server that hot-updates Velotype apps.

Every example in these docs is a file that is type-checked against the published package and run, and the output shown is what the example printed. veloserver also logs its own messages when it starts, stops, and mounts files. Those are not shown.

## Install

veloserver is a [JSR package](https://jsr.io/@velotype/veloserver) for Deno:

```sh
deno add jsr:@velotype/veloserver
```

## A server

A `Router` holds routes, and a `Server` serves a router. `serve(hostname, port)` calls `Deno.serve()`. The server needs `--allow-net` and no other permission to serve:

```sh
deno run --allow-net server.ts
```

```tsx
import { Router, Server } from "@velotype/veloserver"

const router = new Router<never>({})

router.get("/", () => {
    const response = new Response("<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>Hello veloserver!</body></html>")
    response.headers.set("content-type", "text/html; charset=utf-8")
    return response
})

// A Server wraps a Router. serve() starts it with Deno.serve() on a hostname and port.
// The server needs --allow-net and no other permission to serve.
const server = new Server(router)
server.serve("127.0.0.1", 3201)

const response = await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:3201/")
console.log(response.status, response.headers.get("content-type"))
console.log(await response.text())

server.close()
```
Output:

```text
200 text/html; charset=utf-8
<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>Hello veloserver!</body></html>
```
The `<never>` in `new Router<never>({})` is the type of the router's [request metadata](/docs/veloserver/request-metadata/). `never` means this router has none.

## Next steps

* [Routes](/docs/veloserver/routes/): paths, path variables, wildcards, and error responses
* [Request metadata](/docs/veloserver/request-metadata/): typed data for each request
* [Inspectors](/docs/veloserver/inspectors/): code that runs before and after handlers
* [Static files](/docs/veloserver/static-files/): serving a directory
* [Running the server](/docs/veloserver/running-the-server/): shutting down, and the development server

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/veloserver/routes/

# Routes

`get()`, `head()`, and `post()` add a handler for a path, or for several paths when given an array. A handler receives the `Request` and its `Context`, and returns a `Response` or a Promise of one.

## Paths

* `:name` matches one path segment and stores it as a path variable, read with `context.pathVariables?.get("name")`
* `*` at the end of a path matches any remaining segments
* A static segment takes priority over a path variable or a wildcard at the same position

```tsx
import { Router, Server } from "@velotype/veloserver"

const router = new Router<never>({})

// A handler receives the request and its Context, and returns a Response or a Promise of one
router.get("/", () => new Response("home"))

// :name matches one path segment and stores it as a path variable
router.get("/users/:id", (request, context) => {
    return router.json(request, context, {id: context.pathVariables?.get("id")})
})

// A static segment takes priority over a path variable at the same position
router.get("/users/me", () => new Response("the current user"))

// * at the end of a path matches any remaining segments
router.get("/files/*", (_request, context) => new Response(`file: ${context.getPathParts().slice(2).join("/")}`))

// An array adds the same handler for several paths
router.get(["/docs/*", "/guides/*"], () => new Response("documentation"))

// Handlers can be async
router.get("/slow", async () => {
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 10))
    return new Response("done waiting")
})

// head() and post() add handlers for HEAD and POST
router.head("/", () => new Response(null, {headers: {"x-head": "yes"}}))
router.post("/echo", async (request) => new Response(await request.text()))

const server = new Server(router)
server.serve("127.0.0.1", 3202)

const base = "http://127.0.0.1:3202"
const show = async (label: string, request: Promise<Response>) => {
    const response = await request
    console.log(`${label}: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`)
}
await show("GET /", fetch(`${base}/`))
await show("GET /users/42", fetch(`${base}/users/42`))
await show("GET /users/me", fetch(`${base}/users/me`))
await show("GET /files/a/b.txt", fetch(`${base}/files/a/b.txt`))
await show("GET /guides/intro", fetch(`${base}/guides/intro`))
await show("GET /slow", fetch(`${base}/slow`))
await show("POST /echo", fetch(`${base}/echo`, {method: "POST", body: "hello"}))
console.log("HEAD /:", (await fetch(`${base}/`, {method: "HEAD"})).headers.get("x-head"))

server.close()
```
Output:

```text
GET /: 200 home
GET /users/42: 200 {"id":"42"}
GET /users/me: 200 the current user
GET /files/a/b.txt: 200 file: a/b.txt
GET /guides/intro: 200 documentation
GET /slow: 200 done waiting
POST /echo: 200 hello
HEAD /: yes
```
## Responses

`router.json(request, context, data)` returns a JSON response with status 200.

## Error responses

The Router options set the handlers for the cases a route cannot handle. Each has a default:

| Option | Used when |
|---|---|
| `not_found_handler` | No route matches the path |
| `bad_request_error_handler` | A handler returns `router.badRequest()`. The router never calls it on its own |
| `server_error_handler` | A handler throws, or returns `router.serverError()` |

`router.badRequest(request, context)` and `router.serverError(request, context)` return the router's own error responses, so a handler can send them. An error that a handler throws is logged.

```tsx
import { Router, Server } from "@velotype/veloserver"

// The Router options set the handlers for unmatched paths, for badRequest(), and for errors thrown by handlers
const router = new Router<never>({
    not_found_handler: () => new Response("Nothing here", {status: 404}),
    bad_request_error_handler: () => new Response("That request was malformed", {status: 400}),
    server_error_handler: () => new Response("Something went wrong", {status: 500}),
})

router.get("/explode", () => {
    throw new Error("a handler threw")
})

// badRequest() and serverError() return the router's own error responses
router.get("/check", (request, context) => {
    return new URL(request.url).searchParams.has("id") ? new Response("ok") : router.badRequest(request, context)
})
router.get("/fail", (request, context) => router.serverError(request, context))

const server = new Server(router)
server.serve("127.0.0.1", 3203)

const base = "http://127.0.0.1:3203"
for (const path of ["/missing", "/explode", "/check", "/check?id=1", "/fail"]) {
    const response = await fetch(base + path)
    console.log(`${path}: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`)
}

server.close()
```
Output:

```text
/missing: 404 Nothing here
/explode: 500 Something went wrong
/check: 400 That request was malformed
/check?id=1: 200 ok
/fail: 500 Something went wrong
```

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/veloserver/request-metadata/

# Request metadata

`Context.meta` holds typed metadata for each request. It is useful for data that a request needs from start to finish, such as a start time, an authenticated user, or a request id.

The Router's type parameter is the metadata type, and the `context_metadata_constructor` option creates it from each request. The metadata is created before any inspector or handler runs.

```tsx
import { Router, Server } from "@velotype/veloserver"

// Context.meta holds typed metadata for each request. The Router's type parameter is its type,
// and context_metadata_constructor creates it from the request.
type Metadata = {startTime: number, requestNumber: number}

let requests = 0
const router = new Router<Metadata>({
    context_metadata_constructor: () => ({startTime: performance.now(), requestNumber: ++requests}),
})

router.get("/users/:id", (request, context) => {
    return router.json(request, context, {
        request: context.meta.requestNumber,
        id: context.pathVariables?.get("id"),
        // The URL is parsed on first access, so a request that never reads it never pays for the parse
        path: context.url.pathname,
        parts: context.getPathParts(),
    })
})

const server = new Server(router)
server.serve("127.0.0.1", 3204)

console.log(await (await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:3204/users/7")).text())
console.log(await (await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:3204/users/8")).text())

server.close()
```
Output:

```text
{"request":1,"id":"7","path":"/users/7","parts":["","users","7"]}
{"request":2,"id":"8","path":"/users/8","parts":["","users","8"]}
```
## Context

A `Context<ContextMetadata>` is created for each request and passed to every inspector and handler.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `meta` | The metadata the router's `context_metadata_constructor` created |
| `pathVariables?: Map<string, string>` | The path variables the route captured, if any |
| `url: URL` | The request's URL, parsed on first access and then cached, so a request that never reads it never pays for the parse |
| `getPathParts(): string[]` | `url.pathname.split("/")` |
| `addPathVariable(name, value)` | Captures a path variable |

Metadata is also how an inspector hands data to a handler: see [Inspectors](/docs/veloserver/inspectors/).

---

Source: https://velotype.github.io/docs/veloserver/inspectors/

# Inspectors

An `Inspector` runs before and after the handlers of a path. It is a pair of functions, and both are optional:

* A **request inspector** runs before the handler. It returns a `RequestInspectorResponse`. An empty one continues to the handler. One with a `response` ends the request early, and that response starts the response chain
* A **response inspector** runs after the handler, and sees each response. It can read or change the response, and returns nothing

`new Inspector(requestInspector?, responseInspector?, observeChildPaths = true)`

By default an inspector also runs for the paths below its own. Pass `false` as the third argument to inspect only its own path.

Use `addGetInspector()`, `addHeadInspector()`, or `addPostInspector()` to add an inspector for one HTTP method, and `addAllInspector()` for GET, HEAD, and POST. Each takes a path or an Array of paths. The path `""` is the root, so an inspector there sees every request.

```tsx
import { Inspector, RequestInspectorResponse, Router, Server } from "@velotype/veloserver"

type Metadata = {startTime?: number}
const router = new Router<Metadata>({context_metadata_constructor: () => ({})})

// An Inspector runs before and after the handlers of a path. Its request inspector can answer the
// request itself, by returning a RequestInspectorResponse with a response, and its response
// inspector sees each response. Both are optional.
router.addAllInspector("", new Inspector<Metadata>(
    (_request, context) => {
        context.meta.startTime = performance.now()
        return new RequestInspectorResponse()
    },
    (request, response, context) => {
        const elapsed = performance.now() - context.meta.startTime!
        console.log(`logged: ${response.status} ${request.method} ${new URL(request.url).pathname} (took ${elapsed < 1000 ? "under a second" : "too long"})`)
    },
))

// A request inspector that returns a response ends the request early. By default an inspector also
// runs for the paths below its own (observeChildPaths), and the third argument turns that off.
router.addGetInspector("/admin", new Inspector<Metadata>(
    (request) => request.headers.get("authorization") == "secret"
        ? new RequestInspectorResponse()
        : new RequestInspectorResponse(new Response("Not allowed", {status: 401})),
))

router.get("/", () => new Response("public"))
router.get("/admin/dashboard", () => new Response("the dashboard"))

// addGetInspector(), addHeadInspector(), addPostInspector(), and addAllInspector() choose the methods
router.addPostInspector("/", new Inspector<Metadata>(undefined, (_request, response) => {
    response.headers.set("x-inspected", "post")
}))
```
